function.name: generate_report
function.description: Generates a comprehensive report based on user activity data within a specified time frame. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

user_id.description: The unique identifier for the user.

start_date.description: The start date for the report period in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD'.

end_date.description: The end date for the report period, inclusive, in the format 'YYYY-MM-DD'.

include_inactive.description: Flag to determine if inactive users should be included in the report.

report_format.description: The format in which the report will be generated.

message.content:
**Ionisation methods – a quick guide** | Ionisation technique | Typical application | Key advantages | Common limitations | |----------------------|---------------------|----------------|--------------------| | **Electron Ionisation (EI)** | Gas‑phase MS of small, volatile molecules (e.g., organic solvents, pesticides) | • Hard ionisation → rich fragmentation pattern (useful for structural elucidation)
• Well‑established library database | • Requires volatile, thermally stable analytes
• Not suitable for large biomolecules | | **Chemical Ionisation (CI)** | Similar to EI but gentler; used for semi‑volatile organics | • Softer than EI → less fragmentation, often gives molecular ion | • Still limited to volatile/semi‑volatile compounds
• Requires a reagent gas (CH₄, NH₃, etc.) | | **Electrospray Ionisation (ESI)** | Proteins, peptides, nucleic acids, metabolites in LC‑MS | • Very soft, produces multiply charged ions → allows high‑molecular‑weight species
• Compatible with aqueous solutions | • Suppression effects in complex matrices
• Requires a liquid chromatography step | | **Matrix‑Assisted Laser Desorption/Ionisation (MALDI)** | Proteomics, polymers, large biomolecules | • Rapid, high‑throughput
• Minimal sample prep | • Requires a suitable matrix
• Limited to surface‑analysis (no chromatographic separation) | | **Atmospheric Pressure Photoionisation (APPI)** | Non‑polar, aromatic compounds | • Works well for non‑polar analytes that are difficult for ESI
• Can be coupled to LC | • Requires a UV lamp
• Less common than ESI | | **Atmospheric Pressure Chemical Ionisation (APCI)** | Semi‑polar, low‑molecular‑weight compounds | • Good for moderately polar analytes
• Works with LC‑MS | • Less sensitive than ESI for highly polar compounds | | **Laser Ablation/Desorption Ionisation (LAI)** | Solid samples, materials analysis | • Direct analysis of solids
• Minimal sample prep | • Requires specialized laser equipment | | **Field‑Ionisation (FII)** | Small molecules, high‑resolution MS | • Very soft, minimal fragmentation
• High mass accuracy | • Requires high vacuum
• Limited throughput | --- ### How to choose the “best” method 1. **Sample type & volatility** * Volatile, small molecules → EI or CI. * Large biomolecules (proteins, peptides) → ESI or MALDI. * Non‑polar aromatics → APPI. 2. **Desired information** * Structural elucidation → hard ionisation (EI) gives rich fragmentation. * Molecular weight determination of large species → soft ionisation (ESI, MALDI). 3. **Instrumentation & workflow** * If you already have an LC‑MS system → ESI or APCI/APPI are plug‑in. * For rapid screening of many samples → MALDI‑TOF. 4. **Matrix effects & sensitivity** * ESI is prone to ion suppression in complex matrices; use sample cleanup or alternative ionisation (APCI). * MALDI can suffer from uneven matrix crystallisation; careful spotting improves reproducibility. 5. **Cost & maintenance** * EI/CI require a vacuum system and electron source; relatively low maintenance. * ESI/APCI/APPI need a nebuliser and high‑voltage power supply; more consumables (solvents, gases). * MALDI needs a laser and matrix reagents; laser maintenance can be costly. --- ### Quick decision tree ``` ┌───────────────────────┐ │ Is the analyte a large biomolecule? ──► Yes → ESI or MALDI │ No │ ├─ Is the analyte volatile? ──► Yes → EI or CI │ No │ ├─ Is the analyte non‑polar aromatic? ──► Yes → APPI │ No │ └─ Default → ESI (most versatile for LC‑MS) ``` --- #### Bottom line There isn’t a single “best” ionisation method; the optimal choice depends on: * **Molecular size & polarity** * **Desired analytical outcome** (fragmentation vs. intact ion) * **Instrument availability** * **Sample complexity & throughput needs** If you give me more details about your analytes, matrix, and analytical goals, I can narrow it down further!
